stories.headline: Jefferson County jury convicts Brandon Mumma of tampering with body of Denver hairstylist Jax Gratton
stories.summary:
A Jefferson County jury on Thursday found Brandon David Mumma, 44, guilty of tampering with a deceased human body and tampering with evidence in the death of Jax Gratton, a Denver hairstylist. Jurors deliberated for only a few hours. Mumma had pleaded not guilty to both counts on June 5.

Gratton, 34, was last seen on the evening of April 15, 2025, and her roommate reported her missing. Her body was found two months later. Prosecutors said Mumma was the last person with her before her death. The March 11 indictment alleges that Gratton and Mumma entered his office at 9655 W. Colfax Avenue at 10:41 p.m. that night. A second man, who has cooperated with police and is not believed to be criminally involved, left with Mumma at 1:43 a.m. on April 16, leaving Gratton alone and asleep under the influence of drugs, according to prosecutors.

A toxicology report found methamphetamine, THC, citalopram and trazodone in her system. Because so much time had passed, coroners could not determine a cause of death. An overdose could neither be proven nor ruled out, and the manner of death was ruled undetermined. Surveillance video showed Mumma returning the next morning, staying about an hour and then throwing trash bags into a dumpster. He told police Gratton had taken too much GHB and passed out before he left her.

stories.headline: Republican lawmakers sue to block Amendment 87 graduated income tax
stories.summary:
Two Republican state senators, Barbara Kirkmeyer of Brighton and Byron Pelton of Sterling, filed a lawsuit Thursday seeking to stop Colorado's new graduated income tax from taking effect. The suit is backed by Advance Colorado, a conservative nonprofit that does not disclose its donors. It argues that Amendment 87 violates the Taxpayer's Bill of Rights, or TABOR.

Voters approved the measure in November. It replaces the state's flat 4.4% income tax with a six-bracket system beginning with tax year 2027, with rates ranging from 3.7% on income up to $25,000 to 8.4% above $1 million. It is expected to raise more than $2 billion a year for education, child care and health care. It raises taxes on households and businesses earning more than about $500,000 and cuts them for those earning less.

The lawsuit contends TABOR required the measure to be split into two ballot questions, one to raise taxes and one to delete TABOR's ban on graduated rates. It also claims voters were misled by the state's nonpartisan voter guide, the blue book, citing a table showing people earning $500,000 to $1 million would receive a tax cut. The state Title Board and Supreme Court previously allowed the measure onto the ballot over a single-subject challenge.

stories.headline: Labor, AI and Medicaid expected to shape Colorado's 2027 legislative session
stories.summary:
With the 2027 legislative session less than two months away, lawmakers are preparing for a new governor for the first time in nearly a decade and Democratic supermajorities in both chambers. Several policy fights are expected to return.

Democrats are expected to make a third attempt to eliminate the Labor Peace Act, an 83-year-old law that requires employees at unionized workplaces to hold two elections to establish a union security agreement. Gov. Jared Polis vetoed the repeal measure in 2025 and again in 2026, citing concerns about mandatory dues deduction. Sen. Julie Gonzales, the 2026 sponsor, will not return, but supporters say the bill, dubbed the Worker Protection Act, will be back.

Gov.-elect Phil Weiser has not said clearly whether he would sign it. He has called the law antiquated while acknowledging business concerns about competitiveness. With supermajorities, Democrats could override a veto regardless.

Lawmakers are also expected to revisit artificial intelligence data centers. Two bills last session, one on environmental effects and one on economic aspects, failed. The debate has intensified since the session ended in May, and some lawmakers hint at more attempts at regulation. Medicaid is also expected to be a focus.

stories.headline: Denver Public Schools board appoints Caron Blanke to District 3 seat
stories.summary:
The Denver Public Schools Board of Education voted 4-2 on Thursday to appoint Caron Blanke to the vacant District 3 seat, ending a 49-day process. Board President Xóchitl Gaytán and member Marlene De La Rosa voted no. John Youngquist, Kimberlee Sia, Amy Klein Molk and Monica Hunter voted yes. Blanke beat finalists Veronica Figoli and Barclay Jones.

Blanke finished as runner-up to DJ Torres in the 2025 District 3 election, with nearly 37% of the vote. Torres resigned last month, saying too much of his time and energy was consumed by internal conflict. His resignation came the day the board was to consider investigating him for alleged member misconduct. The board had earlier denied a bid by former member Scott Esserman to reclaim the seat.

Blanke is a consultant for several early childhood centers in the Denver area, a former chair of the collaborative school committee at the Denver School of the Arts and a DPS parent. Under Colorado law, an appointee serves only until the next election, so she will hold the seat for one year and must run in 2027 to stay on. She is to be sworn in Nov. 20, and her first meeting as a member is Nov. 30.

stories.headline: Colorado Economic Development Commission approves $14.5 million in job incentives for five companies
stories.summary:
The Colorado Economic Development Commission on Thursday approved up to about $14.5 million in performance-based job growth incentive tax credits for five companies considering expansions in the state. To receive the credits, each company must meet job creation and retention requirements over eight years. Projects carry code names to protect company identities during the competitive process.

The largest package, up to $6.4 million, went to Project Segundo, a Colorado-headquartered critical minerals processing company. It expects to invest more than $300 million in a manufacturing facility with up to three production lines. It is considering Adams County, where it would create 243 jobs at an average wage of $96,624, about 130% of the county average. It is also weighing Georgia and Texas.

Project Primero, tied to the same company, received up to $1.5 million to expand research and headquarters operations in Boulder County. It would create 48 jobs averaging $101,771, and Georgia is also under consideration. Project Cobalt Blue was approved for up to $3 million. The company synthesizes chemicals such as propellants, fuel and explosives from nonpetroleum feedstocks and conducts rare-earth separation. State staff said the projects would reinforce Colorado's leadership in critical minerals.

stories.headline: Colorado submits bid to host proposed U.S. Space Academy in Colorado Springs
stories.summary:
Colorado formally submitted its proposal Monday to host a proposed United States Space Academy, pitching Banning Lewis Ranch in eastern Colorado Springs as the site of a projected $8.2 billion permanent campus. President Donald Trump signed an executive order in August to start creating the NASA-led federal academy, and NASA soon issued a request for information from interested states.

The 100-page bid highlights Colorado's aerospace industry, Space Force bases and programs at CU Boulder, the Colorado School of Mines and the Air Force Academy. The 508-acre site includes a 321-acre campus and a 187-acre innovation district for research and industry partners. State officials call the site shovel-ready and under a single owner, Norwood Development Group, which would sell or lease the academy grounds to NASA.

If selected, the state says it could break ground next year. About 300 students would begin studies at UCCS in fall 2028, with the permanent campus finished by 2031 for 1,200 students and eventual growth to 4,000. Construction is estimated at $6.1 billion in today's dollars, rising to $8.2 billion with cost increases. The state outlines about $320 million in financing and tax incentives. Lt. Gov. Dianne Primavera chaired the bid committee, and Colorado faces stiff competition from other states.

stories.headline: Colorado reports clade I mpox case in Denver metro resident
stories.summary:
Colorado public health officials have reported a case of mpox, formerly known as monkeypox, in a Denver metro-area resident. The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment did not say where in the metro area the person lives, citing privacy. The case is one of more than 200 the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has tracked in at least 31 states and Puerto Rico.

The resident contracted clade I, a type that has recently begun spreading in the United States. Clade II was responsible for the 2022 outbreak and continues to circulate. Many of the national cases are believed to have been contracted domestically rather than through international travel.

Symptoms include rashes or bumps on the hands, feet, chest, face, mouth or near the genitals. The virus spreads mainly through close physical contact, including direct contact with an infected person's sores or lesions, and is unlikely to spread through brief interactions without contact. Gay and bisexual men, transgender women and gender-diverse people have faced higher risk in the current outbreak.

State epidemiologist Dr. Rachel Herlihy said the risk to the general public remains low. She encouraged those at increased risk to consider vaccination, noting the Jynneos vaccine protects against both clades. Recent cases have been relatively mild, with no reported deaths.

topStory.headline: Mayor Mamdani Unveils Plan to Close Rikers Island by End of 2032, Over Five Years After Legal Deadline
topStory.summary:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Friday unveiled what his administration called the city's first comprehensive plan to close the Rikers Island jail complex, setting a goal of ending all incarceration at the facility and relocating its remaining population by the end of 2032. The plan outlines investments including $146 million from the city next fiscal year for mental health care, substance use treatment, educational and vocational programming inside jails and in communities, and victim services. AMNY reported the plan outlines $290 million in total investments aimed at reducing the jail population by nearly 40%.

Under the schedule, the first of four planned borough-based jails would open in Brooklyn in 2029, followed by facilities in the Bronx and Queens in 2031 and Manhattan in 2032. Together with three hospital-based therapeutic housing units, the new system would have a capacity of about 4,500 beds, compared with roughly 6,600 people held on Rikers as of early November. The administration aims to cut the population to no more than 5,500 when the Brooklyn jail opens and no more than 4,100 by the end of 2032. It also seeks to open therapeutic units at Woodhull Hospital in Brooklyn and North Central Bronx Hospital, providing 236 beds, in 2028, a year earlier than expected, and to reduce the planned women's facility in Queens from 450 beds to 250, reversing an increase made under former Mayor Eric Adams. A 104-bed therapeutic unit opened at Bellevue Hospital in April.

"It is time to finally close Rikers Island," Mamdani said in a statement, adding that the plan would also address pretrial detention and case delays that deprive people of their right to a speedy trial. In a separate statement he said the city has "a legal and moral obligation to close Rikers." Council Speaker Julie Menin said delays under previous administrations had made clear that more time was needed to fulfill the commitment the Council made in 2019.

The plan arrives amid a legal mandate to close Rikers by Aug. 31, 2027, established by legislation passed by the City Council in 2019 and signed by then-Mayor Bill de Blasio. That law called for replacing Rikers with four smaller borough-based jails in Brooklyn, the Bronx, Queens and Manhattan. The city is not on track to meet the deadline because construction is behind schedule and the jail population has risen since 2020, raising concerns about whether it can be reduced enough to fit the new facilities. The closure effort has spanned three mayoral administrations and repeated setbacks since the city formally committed to it in 2017.

Meeting the new timeline will require completing construction, significantly reducing the number of people in custody, securing cooperation from prosecutors and the state court system, and amending the existing law. City Hall said the Council would introduce legislation to revise the deadline, though a city official did not provide a timetable. The administration said it is confident it can reduce the population sufficiently but did not outline a contingency plan if the number in custody still exceeds capacity in 2032. The plan states the administration will work with the City Council, the remediation manager, the federal monitor and the Board of Correction, and it also includes modernizing the Department of Correction and planning for future reuse of the island.
